title: Government seeks to reduce US tariff during Trump visit
summary: The Philippines wants to see a reduction in the 12.5 percent tariff being imposed on its exports to the United States when President Marcos and US President Donald Trump meet in Manila this week.

blocks.text: Youth groups join the ‘Kampuhan sa Liwasang Bonifacio’ of different indigenous groups in Manila on November 16, 2026, to protest US President Donald Trump’s visit.

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines wants to see a reduction in the 12.5 percent tariff being imposed on its exports to the United States when President Marcos and US President Donald Trump meet in Manila this week.

At a press conference yesterday following the conclusion of the 28th Association of the Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Economic Community Council gathering, Trade Secretary Cristina Roque said the 12.5 percent tariff imposed by the US on Philippine exports would be among the topics to be discussed during the bilateral meeting between Marcos and Trump.
“Of course my wish is to bring down the tariff,” she said. “That’s really what [we want] because we want to be able to expand the exports to the US and to all other markets globally.”
Last July, the US imposed a 12.5 percent tariff on goods from the Philippines and other economies to make up for gaps in prohibiting imports produced with forced labor.
The 12.5 percent tariff replaced the 10 percent levy earlier slapped on Philippine exports to the US after the US Supreme Court declared as unconstitutional the reciprocal tariffs imposed last year.
In July, the trade, finance and labor departments signed a joint administrative order (JAO) establishing a mechanism for investigating and blocking imports produced through forced labor.

Under the JAO, an inter-agency committee was created to evaluate and conduct a probe on complaints on imports suspected to have been produced through forced labor. Roque said the US has received a copy of the JAO.
“We will be discussing actually on Nov. 18 all of this,” she said.
Earlier, Trade Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo said he is “reasonably optimistic” that the JAO to prohibit imports made through forced labor would help lift the 12.5 percent tariff.
The US is the top destination for Philippine merchandise exports, accounting for $13.46 billion or 15.9 percent of the country’s exports last year.
From January to September, the US remained the leading market for Philippine exports of goods with a 20.2 percent share valued at $14.95 billion.
